sermon:
## The Compromise Nobody Called Sin
*How partial obedience becomes the seed of every disaster*

**Text:** Judges 1:1–2:5 · **Supporting:** Exodus 23:32–33 · Deuteronomy 7:2 · Joshua 23:12–13 · 1 Corinthians 5:6

Joshua is dead, and the book of Judges opens like a victory still in motion. Israel asks the right question, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?" (Judges 1:1). Judah goes up. The Lord gives the land. For a moment it reads like the conquest continuing under its own momentum. Then the language changes, almost too quietly to notice, and the whole future of the nation turns on a single repeated verb.

**The word that names the rot: "did not drive out"**
Read the first chapter slowly and you will hear it like a bell tolling. "Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants" (Judges 1:27). "Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites" (1:29). Zebulun did not. Asher did not. Naphtali did not. And then the verb softens into something worse, "the Canaanites lived among them" becomes "Israel lived among the Canaanites" (1:32–33). The text is tracking a slow inversion. Israel was sent to dispossess; it settles for cohabiting. And the moment it could enforce the command, it did not, "when Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out" (1:28). They had the power. They lacked the will. They chose the deal over the obedience.

Notice what God had said. "You shall make no covenant with them and their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me" (Exodus 23:32–33). Moses had been blunter still: "you shall save alive nothing that breathes" (Deuteronomy 20:16), and the reason was never cruelty for its own sake, it was that "they may not teach you to do according to all their abominable practices" (Deuteronomy 20:18). The command was a quarantine. Israel turned it into a labor arrangement. Forced labor felt like victory. It looked like winning. The Canaanite was under tribute, after all, defeated, manageable, profitable. Nobody at the time would have called it sin. They would have called it pragmatism.

**The angel who shows up to name the breach**
So God sends a messenger, and he does not come with a sword. He comes with a sentence. The angel goes up from Gilgal to Bochim and says, "I brought you up from Egypt... I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you, and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land.' ... But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?" (Judges 2:1–2). And then the verdict that hangs over the next twenty chapters: "So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you" (2:3).

Hear what God is doing. He is naming as covenant breach what Israel had filed under coexistence. The people had not built an altar to Baal. They had not renounced Yahweh. They had simply declined to finish, and declining to finish is the breach. The thorns are not punishment imported from outside. The thorns are the unfinished obedience grown up into a nation. The people weep at Bochim, and they name the place "Weeping," and they sacrifice, and then the very next thing the book records is the cycle beginning. The tears were real. They changed nothing. That is the most frightening sentence in the chapter.

**The mercy that will not let us call it small**
We are tempted to read this as ancient and far away, a tale of swords and Canaanites with no claim on a Tuesday. But the mechanism is the most familiar thing in the world, and I know it because I have run it from a pulpit. The sin we never repent of is not the one we defend. It is the one we have renamed. We do not call it bitterness; we call it standing up for ourselves. We do not call it greed; we call it providing for my family. We do not call it the slow death of a marriage; we call it growing apart. We put the Canaanite to forced labor, we manage the sin, we keep it useful, we tell ourselves it is under control, and we never drive it out, because driving it out costs something the deal does not.

Paul saw exactly this in the church at Corinth and reached for the kitchen: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" (1 Corinthians 5:6). Not most of the lump. The whole lump. A little is enough, because sin is not a quantity you tolerate. It is a yeast that works. The Canaanite Israel kept for labor became the god its grandchildren served. The compromise nobody called sin in chapter one becomes the child sacrifice nobody can stop by chapter eleven. This is how it always goes. Not in a leap. In a verb, did not drive out, repeated until it owns you.

Here is where the gospel stands or the whole story is only despair. Joshua could give Israel the land. He could not give them a heart that would finish. There is a greater Joshua, the name is the same name, Yeshua, and where Israel left the work half done, He cried "It is finished" (John 19:30) and meant it. He did not put our sin to forced labor. He drove it out, into His own body on the tree, and left nothing alive that breathes against us. The thorns that should have been in our side were pressed instead into His brow. That is the only obedience that was ever complete, and it was not ours.

So the angel's question is still standing in the room, and it has your name on it now. What is this you have done? Not the sin you confess. The one you have renamed.

Partial obedience is disobedience that waits.

## The Cycle Named in Advance
*The whole machine of Judges, pulled back into view*

**Text:** Judges 2:6–3:6 · **Supporting:** Exodus 1:8 · Psalm 106:43–45 · Romans 1:24 · Hebrews 3:12

Most of the time the Bible shows you the trees and trusts you to find the forest. Here, just once, the narrator climbs the hill and shows you the whole forest before the first tree falls. Judges 2:6–3:6 is the architect's blueprint for everything that follows, the cycle named in advance, so that when Othniel and Ehud and Gideon and Samson come, you already know the shape of the machine grinding underneath them.

**A generation that did not know**
It begins with a death and a forgetting. "Joshua... died... And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the Lord or the work that he had done for Israel" (Judges 2:8–10). Sit with the word *know*. It is not that they had never heard the stories. They had the stories. They did not have the knowing, the covenant intimacy, the memory that grips the will. There is a haunting echo here, deliberate, of the opening of Exodus, where "there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph" (Exodus 1:8). A king who did not know became Israel's bondage. A generation that did not know becomes Israel's undoing. The danger is never that the truth is lost from the shelves. It is that it is lost from the heart while it sits on the shelves.

This is one generation deep. Joshua's people saw the Jordan stand up like a wall. Their grandchildren saw nothing, they only heard about it, and hearing is not the same as knowing, and so the floor gives way in a single hop from one bed to the next. Faith is never inherited. It is always announced again, or it is gone.

**The four turns of the wheel**
Then the narrator lays the gears bare, and they turn the same way every time. First: "The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord and served the Baals" (Judges 2:11). Second: "So the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers... he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies" (2:14). Third: "the Lord raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them" (2:16). Fourth, and this is the gear that grinds: "whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers" (2:19).

Sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, and then back to sin, *worse than before.* It is not a circle. A circle returns to where it started. This is a spiral, and it descends. Every turn of the wheel ends lower than it began. Psalm 106 later sets the same machine to music: "Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity" (Psalm 106:43). The deliverance is real. The deliverance is repeated. And it never cures the disease, it only interrupts the symptom, because the rescuer keeps dying and the heart keeps reverting.

Hear the verb that should stop your breath: God "gave them over." It returns in Romans, where Paul diagnoses humanity itself, "God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts" (Romans 1:24). The worst judgment is not the plunderer at the gate. It is God handing you over to the thing you said you wanted. Israel wanted the Baals. God let them have the Baals, and the Baals had them. There is no punishment more total than getting exactly what you insisted on.

**The cycle you are standing in**
We read this as Israel's pattern and we miss that it is the human pattern, and I miss it most when I am most sure I have outgrown it. We do not serve carved Baals. We serve the more sophisticated kind. We do what is evil, comfort, control, the approval that functions as a god. We are handed over, to the anxiety, the addiction, the slow hardening, and we cry out, and a deliverance comes, a good week, a moved conviction, a tearful Sunday. And then the conviction dies the way the judge died, and we turn back more corrupt than before. The same sin. Worse this time. Because the wheel only knows one direction.

The writer of Hebrews looked at this exact stretch of Israel's history and turned it into a warning aimed straight at the church: "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12). He is not worried about the people outside the covenant. He is worried about the people inside it, in the pew, who know the stories and have lost the knowing. That is the most dangerous place to stand, close enough to be familiar, far enough to be lost.

And here is why the book of Judges is finally not despair, though it reads like despair for twenty-one chapters. Every judge dies, and the cycle resumes, and the whole book is screaming a question it cannot answer: who will break the wheel? Not a better judge. The wheel ate the best of them. Israel does not need another rescuer who dies and leaves them to revert. It needs a Judge who will not die and leave them, or who will die and not stay dead, and rise to put a new heart in the very people who keep turning back. "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33). That is the only thing that ever stops the spiral: not a rescue from outside the heart, but a rewriting of the heart itself. Judges is the eight-hundred-year argument for why we needed Him.

The cycle is named in advance because you were meant to recognize it. You have lived it.

We forget faster than He saves.

## Three Deliverers and a Borrowed Strength
*The rescue belongs to the Lord, even when the rescuer is nobody*

**Text:** Judges 3:7–31 · **Supporting:** Zechariah 4:6 · 1 Corinthians 1:27 · 2 Corinthians 12:9 · Psalm 44:3

The first three judges arrive almost in a hurry, Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, and if you read quickly you will miss what God is teaching before the famous names show up. He is establishing the grammar of the whole book in three short paragraphs. The deliverer is not the deliverance. The strength is borrowed. The rescue is the Lord's, and He proves it by choosing the kind of rescuer no one would have bet on.

**Othniel: the Spirit, not the swordsman**
The cycle turns for the first time. Israel forgets the Lord and serves the Baals, God sells them to Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia, they cry out, and God raises up Othniel. And the text is careful to tell you exactly where his strength comes from before it tells you anything else: "The Spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the Lord gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand" (Judges 3:10). Not Othniel's tactics. Not Othniel's army. "The Spirit of the Lord was upon him", that clause is the engine, and the victory is just the exhaust. The land has rest forty years, and Othniel dies, and the spiral resumes. He was a vessel, not a savior. The book is teaching you to look past the hand to the One who fills it.

**Ehud: the man the enemy never saw coming**
Then it gets strange, and the strangeness is the sermon. Israel is enslaved to Eglon, king of Moab, a man so fat the text will not let you forget it, and God raises up a deliverer the narrator describes with one telling detail: "Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man" (Judges 3:15). Benjamin means "son of the right hand," and here is a Benjaminite who is left-handed, already a man defined by what he is not. He makes a sword "a cubit in length" and straps it on his right thigh, the side no guard would check on a right-handed world's assumption. He brings the tribute, sends his men away, and tells the king, "I have a secret message for you, O king" (3:19). Eglon rises from his cool roof chamber. Ehud reaches with his left hand, draws from his right thigh, and "thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade" (3:21–22). The deliverance of Israel turns on a left hand no one thought to watch.

Do not rush past the comedy and miss the theology. God routes a nation's freedom through a man's so-called weakness, the wrong-handed Benjaminite, the overlooked detail, the thing everyone discounted. The Lord does not borrow the king's right-hand champion. He takes the left-handed man and the unguarded thigh, precisely so that no one can say the strong arm of Israel saved Israel.

**Shamgar: an ox goad and a footnote**
And then the smallest deliverer of all, in a single verse so brief it almost feels like an afterthought: "After him was Shamgar... who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel" (Judges 3:31). No genealogy. No Spirit clause spelled out. No forty years of rest recorded. A farmer's cattle prod, a sharpened stick, and six hundred dead Philistines, and the verdict the narrator will not withhold: "he also saved Israel." A man with the wrong weapon and no résumé saves the people of God.

**The strength was never yours**
Here is the pattern God is hammering into the foundation of the book before the foundation can crack. The underdog. The left-handed man. The farmer with a stick. Three rescuers, and not one of them had the strength the job required. The strength was borrowed, from the Spirit who came upon Othniel, from the providence that armed Ehud's overlooked side, from the God who can make an ox goad lethal. Centuries later the prophet would compress the whole lesson into one line for Zerubbabel: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). And Paul, looking at a church full of nobodies, said it plain: "God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong... so that no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

Now turn the mirror, because we are the Israel that wants a champion with the right hand and the full résumé. We trust the strong thing. We trust the gifted leader, the big platform, the impressive deliverer, and we are quietly embarrassed by the left-handed man and the ox goad. And God keeps refusing to work the way we would respect, because the moment the strength is ours, the glory is ours, and He shares His glory with no one. I have wanted to be the right-handed champion in my own ministry, competent, impressive, the strength visibly mine, and that wanting is the very thing that disqualifies the work. "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Not despite your weakness. In it.

And this is the road that runs straight to a cross, where God saved the whole world through the most overlooked rescuer of all, a carpenter, executed on the wrong side of the empire, defeating death with the ultimate ox goad of a Roman gallows. The Deliverer who looked like no deliverer at all. "I will not trust in my bow, nor can my sword save me" (Psalm 44:6). It never could. The arm of flesh fails, every time, and that failure is the mercy that drives you to the only strength that holds.

The strength was never theirs.

## The Glory Goes to a Woman
*God routes the victory through the hands no man expected*

**Text:** Judges 4–5 · **Supporting:** 1 Samuel 2:8 · Isaiah 42:8 · 1 Corinthians 1:29 · Luke 1:52

Twenty years under Jabin and his nine hundred iron chariots, and Israel cries out again. The deliverance God sends comes with a deliberate, almost provocative design, the honor of the day will land in the hands of women, so that when the dust settles, no man can stand over the battlefield and call the victory his. This is not an accident of the narrative. It is the point of the narrative.

**Barak's condition and the price of it**
Deborah is already there when the chapter opens, "a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time" (Judges 4:4), sitting under her palm while Israel comes to her for judgment. She summons Barak and delivers the word of God plainly: take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor, and "I will draw out Sisera... with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand" (4:7). The command is clear. The promise is total. And Barak hedges.

"If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go" (Judges 4:8). There it is, the faith that needs a guarantee it can see, the courage that requires a chaperone. Deborah agrees to go, but she names the cost: "the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman" (4:9). Barak wanted assurance. His hedging cost him the honor. The God who gives the victory decides where the glory lands, and Barak's flinch redirected it away from himself.

**Jael and the tent peg**
The battle is the Lord's from the first sword stroke, "the Lord routed Sisera and all his chariots" (Judges 4:15), and the iron chariots that terrified Israel for twenty years become useless in a flooded valley; the song will say "the torrent Kishon swept them away" (5:21). Sisera, the great general, flees on foot. He runs to the tent of Jael, expecting sanctuary, and she gives him milk and a blanket and the lie of safety. Then, while he sleeps, "Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand... and drove the peg into his temple" (4:21). The commander of nine hundred chariots, undone by a woman's tent peg and a borrowed hammer.

And then Israel sings, and the song of Deborah crowns Jael with a line no warrior gets: "Most blessed of women be Jael... of tent-dwelling women most blessed" (Judges 5:24). The mighty fell, the song says, "between her feet he sank, he fell" (5:27). The general's mother waits at the window for the spoils of war that will never come (5:28). The whole arc of the story bends to put the trophy in a woman's hands.

**The God who will not split the prize**
We should be honest about why this unsettles us. We are the people who want a champion we can admire, the strong man, the decorated general, the hero with the right credentials. And God keeps handing the decisive moment to the people we would have overlooked: a prophetess judging under a tree, a nomad woman with a tent peg. He does it on purpose. He told us why through Isaiah: "I am the Lord; that is my name; my glory I give to no other" (Isaiah 42:8). Not a little of it. None of it. When Barak reached for an arrangement that would have left some of the glory clinging to him, God simply routed the victory around him. He will not split the prize with His own deliverer.

This is the same God Hannah would sing about, "He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap" (1 Samuel 2:8), and the same God Mary would sing about, that He "has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate" (Luke 1:52). It is one song, sung across a thousand years, and it always says the same thing: God lifts the low and humbles the high so that the boasting ends. "None... might boast in the presence of God" (1 Corinthians 1:29).

Now the mirror, and it is a hard one for a man who has spent his life in front of rooms. The instinct that ruined Barak's honor is the instinct I battle every week, the quiet need for the deliverance to have my fingerprints on it, the small bargain that says, I will serve, but let it be on a road that leads to my glory. We dress it up. We call it stewardship of our gifts, building our influence, leaving a legacy. God hears the bargain underneath, and He answers it the way He answered Barak, by handing the decisive thing to someone else, so that the work gets done and the credit goes where it always belonged.

And this points, as everything in Judges finally points, past every human deliverer to the one Deliverer who took the opposite road on purpose. Christ did not hedge. He did not say, I will go if my glory is secured. He emptied Himself, "taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7), and won the only victory that matters by surrendering every claim to honor, and so received "the name that is above every name" (2:9). The way up was the way down. He grasped at nothing, and was given everything. Barak grasped at a guarantee, and lost his name from the song.

So the question stands over your service, the way it stood over Barak's: are you in this for the deliverance, or for the road that leads to your glory? Because God will accomplish the deliverance either way. The only thing in your hands is whose name ends up in the song.

God shares His glory with no man.

## A Coward, a Fleece, and Three Hundred Men
*God whittles us down until the credit can only be His*

**Text:** Judges 6:1–7:25 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 1:29 · 2 Corinthians 4:7 · Isaiah 41:10 · Psalm 20:7

Gideon is the patron saint of weak faith, and that is exactly why the chapter exists. We tend to remember him as a hero. The text remembers him as a frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from raiders, and the joke God tells through the angel is the kindest joke in Scripture. The whole story is about a God patient enough to work with a coward, and jealous enough to make sure no one mistakes the coward for the cause.

**The greeting that was a joke and a promise**
Midian has been stripping Israel bare for seven years, swarming the land like locusts. And the angel of the Lord finds Gideon down in a winepress, hiding his grain, and greets him with a line dripping with holy irony: "The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor" (Judges 6:12). Mighty man of valor, said to a man hiding from the enemy in a hole. Gideon answers exactly as a hiding man would: "if the Lord is with us, why then has all this happened to us?" (6:13). The doubt is right there in the open. And God does not rebuke it. He commissions it: "Go in this might of yours and save Israel... Do not I send you?" (6:14).

Then comes the hedging, and there is a great deal of it, because Gideon is not a brave man pretending to doubt, he is a doubting man being made brave. He asks for a sign and the angel burns up his offering with fire from a rock (6:21). He pulls down his father's altar to Baal, but he does it at night "because he was too afraid" (6:27). And then the famous fleece, not once but twice. "If you will save Israel by my hand... let there be dew on the fleece alone, and on all the ground let it be dry" (6:37). God does it. Then Gideon, knowing he is pressing his luck, asks for the reverse, dry fleece, wet ground, and God does that too (6:39–40). This is not faith at its strongest. This is faith on a crutch, asking God to prove Himself one more time. And God stoops. The patience of God with weak faith is the quiet miracle underneath the loud one.

**Too many men**
Gideon finally raises an army, thirty-two thousand men against the Midianite host. And God says something no general has ever wanted to hear: "The people with you are too many" (Judges 7:2). Too many. And the reason is the thesis of the whole book, stated outright: "lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me'" (7:2). So God starts subtracting. Everyone afraid, go home, twenty-two thousand leave. Ten thousand remain, and God says still too many. He brings them to the water and watches how they drink, and keeps only the three hundred who lap from their hands. From thirty-two thousand to three hundred, less than one percent, marching against an army "like locusts in abundance" (7:12). God did not strengthen Gideon's hand. He weakened it, on purpose, until victory could only be miracle.

And the battle is no battle at all. Three hundred men with trumpets and torches and empty jars, standing in the dark, and at the signal they blow and smash and shout, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon" (Judges 7:20). And the Lord sets every Midianite's sword against his neighbor (7:22). The enemy destroys itself. Israel barely lifts a blade. The weapons were trumpets and clay pots, instruments designed to make noise and break, not to kill, and that is the whole point.

**Treasure in clay jars**
Now look at what you are holding, because the empty jars are about you. Paul reached for this exact image to describe what we are: "we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (2 Corinthians 4:7). You are the clay pot. You were always meant to be breakable. The light is not in the strength of the jar, it shines out precisely when the jar is shattered, the way the torches blazed only when the three hundred smashed the cover hiding them.

We hate this. We are building bigger armies and counting our thirty-two thousand and reading our own strength as God's blessing on us, and all the while God is looking at our numbers and saying, too many. I have done it, measured the work by the size of the crowd, mistaken the full room for the favor of God, quietly proud of a hand that I needed Him to weaken. The mercy of God is often subtraction. He takes away the army you were trusting so that when the deliverance comes you cannot possibly credit the army. "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God" (Psalm 20:7). He removes the chariots so the trust has nowhere to go but Him.

And this is the gospel pressed into the dirt of Gideon's field. God saves through weakness on purpose, so that the credit can only be His, and He brought that pattern to its end at a cross, where the Deliverer of the world looked like total defeat, a man stripped, broken like a clay jar, no army, no power anyone could see. "He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God" (2 Corinthians 13:4). The shattering was the salvation. The breaking was the point. God still says to the hiding, hedging, fleece-asking man, *the Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor*, not because the man is mighty, but because the One who is with him is.

He saves so He gets the credit.

## The Hero Who Could Not Stop Winning
*How a man delivered by grace turns his deliverance into an idol*

**Text:** Judges 8:1–35 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 8:11–14 · 1 Corinthians 10:12 · Galatians 5:7 · Proverbs 30:8–9

The hard truth about Gideon is that the dangerous part of his story comes after the victory, not before it. We can handle a frightened man hiding in a winepress; we know how that story is supposed to go, and God is patient with him in it. What we are not ready for is the man on the other side of the miracle, the same Gideon, now flush with success, who cannot stop winning, and in the winning loses everything the winning was for. Chapter eight is what happens to a delivered man who never let his deliverance finish its work in him.

**The victory turns to vengeance**
The Midianites are routed, but Gideon is still chasing, and the tone has changed. The men of Succoth and Penuel refuse to feed his exhausted troops, hedging their bets in case Gideon loses. They are cowards, and they are wrong. But watch what Gideon does. He does not rebuke them and move on. He vows revenge, runs down the Midianite kings, and then comes back and makes good on it: "he took the elders of the city, and with thorns of the wilderness and with briers he taught the men of Succoth a lesson" (Judges 8:16), and "he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city" (8:17). The man God raised up to save Israel is now flogging and killing Israelites who crossed him.

Then the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and a darker note still. They admit they killed Gideon's brothers, and Gideon says, "If you had saved them alive, I would not kill you" (Judges 8:19). The deliverance has curdled into a blood feud. The Spirit-empowered judge of chapter seven is now settling personal scores in chapter eight, and the text lets you feel the difference. Success did not sanctify him. It exposed him.

**The golden ephod and the snare**
Israel, dazzled, offers Gideon a crown: "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also" (Judges 8:22). And here Gideon says exactly the right thing, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (8:23). For one sentence he is a giant. Then, in the very next breath, he asks each man for a golden earring from the plunder, and from the gold "Gideon made an ephod and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family" (8:27).

Look closely, because the danger here is subtle and that is what makes it deadly. Gideon refused the crown and then built a religious object, an ephod, a priestly thing, a piece of worship, out of the spoils of his greatest victory. He refused political idolatry and manufactured spiritual idolatry. And Israel "whored after it." The word the prophets use for covenant betrayal, *zanah*, lands right here in Gideon's hometown, on a holy-looking thing made from a holy victory. The most dangerous idols are not the ugly ones. They are the ones built out of your spiritual success, the ministry that becomes your name, the win that becomes the thing you serve.

**The unfinished man and the warning Moses gave**
Moses saw this exact trap coming four hundred years earlier, and named it: "Take care lest you forget the Lord your God... lest, when you have eaten and are full... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord" (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). The danger is not the famine. It is the full barn. Gideon survived Midian. He did not survive his own success, and neither do most men. Paul's warning is shorter and just as sharp: "let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). The fall comes after the standing. It always does.

Now the rotation, and I have to put myself in it first, because I have watched men finish badly and I know the soil it grows in. The frightened, dependent version of us, hiding in the winepress, asking for the fleece, that version prays. It knows it needs God. The danger is the version of us that has won something, that has a track record, that has a golden victory to point to. That man stops asking. He builds the ephod. He makes a shrine out of the very thing God did through him, and people start whoring after it, and he lets them, because it has his name on it. The wound underneath Gideon is the wound underneath every unfinished man: he was delivered, but he was never deeply changed, and so the deliverance became his next idol. "Give me neither poverty nor riches... lest I be full and deny you" (Proverbs 30:8–9). The full hand forgets faster than the empty one.

And this is why Judges keeps pointing past every judge to a King who would not curdle in success, who held all power and washed feet with it, who was offered every crown and took a cross instead, who finished His race when Gideon and the rest of us run out of road. "You ran well. Who hindered you?" (Galatians 5:7). Gideon ran well for one chapter and then hindered himself, and the proof is in the last line: the moment he dies, Israel turns back to Baal and "did not show steadfast love to the family of Gideon" (Judges 8:35). He built a shrine to his victory, and it outlived neither him nor his sons. Only one Deliverer ever crossed the finish line with His hands still open. The rest of us need His grip on us, because our own grip always slips somewhere on the back half.

Unfinished men finish badly.

## The Bramble King and the Fire He Started
*Self-made kingship collapses into the fire it kindled*

**Text:** Judges 9:1–57 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 16:18 · Galatians 6:7 · James 3:16 · Hosea 8:4

Gideon refused a crown. His son murdered seventy men to take one nobody had offered him. Chapter nine is the story of Abimelech, and it is the bloodiest, ugliest political story in Judges, a parable of self-made kingship that ends exactly where self-made kingship always ends, in the fire its own ambition lit. The narrator wants you to watch the whole arrangement burn, and to understand that God Himself struck the match back.

**The crown bought with blood**
Abimelech is Gideon's son by a concubine in Shechem, and he is hungry. He goes to his mother's relatives and makes his pitch, better one ruler than seventy of Gideon's sons, and remember, "I am your bone and your flesh" (Judges 9:2). The men of Shechem fund him from the temple of Baal-berith, and with the money "he hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him" (9:4). Then the atrocity: "he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone" (9:5). Seventy executions on a single rock. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes by hiding. A throne is built on a pile of murdered brothers, financed by an idol's treasury and staffed by hired thugs. This is what self-appointed kingship costs, and Abimelech pays it gladly.

**Jotham's parable and the rot it exposes**
The lone survivor climbs Mount Gerizim and shouts down a parable that cuts to the root of the whole thing. The trees go out to anoint a king. The olive tree refuses, it will not give up its oil. The fig tree refuses, it will not give up its sweetness. The vine refuses, it will not give up its wine. The useful, fruitful trees all decline the crown, because they have real work to do. And then: "the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us'" (Judges 9:14). The bramble, a worthless thornbush that bears nothing, good only for catching fire, accepts instantly, and answers with menace: "if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon" (9:15).

The bramble is Abimelech, and the parable exposes the rot precisely. The man who grasps for the crown is the man with nothing to offer, the bramble, not the olive. The fruitful are too busy bearing fruit to chase the throne; only the barren are desperate for it. And the bramble's only gift is fire. A thornbush cannot shade you or feed you. It can only burn, and take everything near it down in the blaze. Jotham names the threat and then runs for his life, leaving a curse hanging in the air: let fire come out from Abimelech and devour Shechem, and from Shechem and devour Abimelech (9:20).

**The fire comes back for the man who lit it**
And it does. Three years later "God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem" (Judges 9:23), and notice, God sent it; this is not random; this is harvest. The alliance turns to civil war. Abimelech razes Shechem and sows it with salt. The people flee to the tower stronghold, and Abimelech piles brushwood against it and burns it down with a thousand inside, the bramble's fire, exactly as Jotham said. Then on to Thebez, another tower, another siege, and there it ends: "a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull" (9:53). Crushed by a woman's millstone, the would-be king begs his armor-bearer to finish him so no one will say a woman killed him. And the narrator drives the verdict home with a hammer: "Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers" (9:56). God returned it. The fire he started came back for him by the hand of God.

This is the law of the harvest, and Scripture states it without softening: "Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). And before the harvest, the pride that plants it: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). James saw the same machine: "where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16). Abimelech is selfish ambition followed to its end. It does not build. It consumes, first the brothers, then the city, then the man himself.

Now turn it, because the bramble lives closer to home than we admit. We read Abimelech as a monster, a far-off tyrant, and miss that ambition without God is the most respectable sin in the room. It wears a suit. It chairs the committee. It calls itself drive, vision, leadership, and underneath, it is the bramble that bears no fruit but cannot stop reaching for the crown, willing to burn whatever it must to get there. I have watched it in church politics and I have felt it in my own chest, the small willingness to advance myself across someone else's ruin and call it calling. Hosea's verdict over Israel's kingmaking is the verdict over all of it: "They made kings, but not through me. They set up princes, but I knew it not" (Hosea 8:4). Kings God never crowned. Thrones He never granted. They always end the same way.

And this is why the book aches, chapter after chapter, for a King who is not a bramble, one who would not grasp the crown but receive it from the Father, who would not start the fire but walk into it, who would not crush His brothers but be crushed for them. "He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities" (Isaiah 53:5). Abimelech was crushed for his own sin, justly, by a millstone. The true King was crushed for the sins of others, mercifully, on a tree. The bramble takes the cedars down with it. The true King lays Himself down so the cedars might live. There is only one safe King, and it is never the one who fought his way up.

Ambition without God consumes its own.

## The Vow He Should Have Broken
*A man who trusted God for victory but not for mercy*

**Text:** Judges 10:1–11:40 · **Supporting:** Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 · Micah 6:6–8 · Hosea 6:6 · Psalm 51:16–17

Jephthah is one of the most tragic figures in Scripture, and the tragedy is sharpened by the fact that he was a genuine man of faith. He is named in the great faith chapter of Hebrews. The Spirit of the Lord came upon him. He won. And then, gripped by a theology of God he had picked up from the nations around him rather than from the covenant, he did something monstrous in the name of devotion, and refused to repent of it. His is the story of a man who trusted God for the battle but not for the mercy, and it cost him his only child.

**The outcast bargained back**
Jephthah begins as a reject. "Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute" (Judges 11:1). His half-brothers drive him out so he will not share the inheritance, and he flees to the land of Tob and gathers a band of "worthless fellows" around him. Then Ammon threatens, and suddenly the elders who exiled him come crawling back: be our leader. There is something raw and human here, Jephthah negotiates, makes them swear, secures his position. The outcast is bargained back into honor. And then the text says the thing that should settle the whole story: "the Spirit of the Lord was upon Jephthah" (11:29). He had everything he needed. God had already taken his side. The victory was assured before he opened his mouth.

**The vow he did not have to make**
But Jephthah does not rest in the Spirit that is already on him. He reaches for a bargaining chip, as if God's favor needed to be purchased: "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return... shall be the Lord's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering" (Judges 11:30–31). This is the fatal sentence, and everything wrong with it is theological. He treats God like the Ammonite gods, a deity to be bribed with blood, bargained with by sacrifice, made to perform by the size of the offering. He already had the Spirit. He did not need to buy what was already given. The vow was unnecessary, and it was pagan to its core.

He wins. He returns. "And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child" (Judges 11:34). His only child, the line lands like a blow. And here is where a true son of the covenant would have repented of a rash and wicked vow. The law of Moses made provision exactly for vows that should not be kept; God never wanted human sacrifice and called it an abomination repeatedly. A vow to do an evil thing is a vow that should be broken, with sorrow, before God who hates the thing more than He honors the oath. But Jephthah tears his clothes and says, "I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot take back my vow" (11:35). He trusted God enough to win the battle. He did not trust God enough to receive mercy for a sinful promise. He kept his word and broke his daughter, and the word should have been the thing that broke.

**What God actually wanted**
This is the heart of it, and it indicts more than Jephthah. God had told Israel for centuries what He wanted, and it was never this. "For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings" (Hosea 6:6). Micah put it as a question and an answer that should have been ringing in Jephthah's ears: "Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression...? He has told you, O man, what is good... to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:7–8). Jephthah gave his firstborn precisely because he did not know the God he served. He knew a God who takes. He did not know the God who gives. And so he murdered the thing he loved most to satisfy a vow that God Himself would have released him from.

Yes, Scripture warns us to keep our vows, "When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it... It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay" (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). But the cure for a rash vow is not a worse sin to honor it. The cure is repentance. Jephthah doubled down where he should have broken down, and that is the trap of a certain kind of grim, joyless religion, it will commit any atrocity rather than admit it was wrong.

Now the mirror, and it is uncomfortably close. We do this. We make God into a vending machine, a deity who responds to our terms, if I do this, He owes me that, and then we honor our own rules even when they are crushing the people we love, because backing down feels like weakness and admitting we were wrong feels like losing. I have seen people destroy their children on the altar of principles God never asked them to keep, and I have done my own smaller versions of it, defending a position long after I knew it was wrong, because I had opened my mouth and could not bear to take it back. That is not faith. A rash vow kept stubbornly is not devotion. It is pride wearing the costume of obedience.

And here is the mercy that breaks the whole tragic logic. There was a Father who did give His only Child, but it was not to satisfy a rash vow He should have broken. It was a deliberate gift of love to a world that could not pay. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). God never wanted Jephthah's daughter. He wanted Jephthah's broken heart, and would have received it gladly. He still does. The God who hates human sacrifice provided the only sacrifice that ever satisfied, and gave it Himself, so that you would never have to bargain again.

A rash vow is not faith.

## The Word That Got Men Killed
*A covenant people turning their swords on each other*

**Text:** Judges 12:1–15 · **Supporting:** Galatians 5:15 · James 4:1 · Proverbs 18:19 · Psalm 133:1

There is a short, brutal chapter sitting right after the tragedy of Jephthah's daughter, and it is easy to skip because it has no famous name and no miracle. But it may be the most damning chapter in the book, because in it Israel's enemy is no longer Midian or Ammon or Philistia. Israel's enemy is Israel. Forty-two thousand of God's covenant people die at the fords of the Jordan, killed by other Israelites, over the pronunciation of one word. This is what the cycle of forgetting finally produces, a nation that turns its army on itself.

**The quarrel that did not have to happen**
Ephraim shows up after the Ammonite war is already won, furious that they were not invited to the fight, and they threaten Jephthah with the same words they once threw at Gideon: "We will burn your house over you with fire" (Judges 12:1). It is a manufactured grievance, wounded pride dressed as principle. Jephthah, fresh from one tragedy and not a man given to patience, answers that he did call and they did not come. The argument escalates. And then a fresh insult: the Ephraimites sneer that the Gileadites are nothing but "fugitives of Ephraim" (12:4), runaways, half-breeds, less than real Israelites. The contempt is the spark. Two tribes of the same covenant, descendants of the same Jacob, heirs of the same promise, and they are reaching for their swords over pride and an insult.

**Shibboleth**
Gilead seizes the fords of the Jordan, the crossing points, and sets up a test. When a fugitive Ephraimite tries to cross, they ask, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he says no, "they said to him, 'Then say Shibboleth,' and he said, 'Sibboleth,' for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan" (Judges 12:6). Shibboleth, a word for a flowing stream, or an ear of grain, and the Ephraimite dialect could not manage the *sh*. So a man's accent became his death sentence. Not his sin. Not his crime. The shape of his vowels. And the toll the narrator records is staggering: "at that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell" (12:6).

Sit with that number against the rest of the book. Gideon delivered Israel with three hundred. Here Israel destroys forty-two thousand of its own. The deliverer-count is in the hundreds; the self-slaughter count is in the tens of thousands. The math is the message. Israel has become more lethal to itself than its enemies ever were. The covenant brothers have learned to detect one another by accent in order to kill more efficiently, a tribal-purity test run at a river crossing, brother butchering brother over a syllable.

**The enemy in the mirror**
What we are watching is the logic of contempt taken to its end, and Scripture diagnoses it without flinching. Paul wrote to a church chewing itself to pieces: "if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). James asked where it comes from: "What causes quarrels and fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1). The Ammonite was the obvious enemy. The deadlier enemy was the passion at war inside Israel itself, the wounded pride, the tribal contempt, the need to be honored. Ephraim was not fighting for God. Ephraim was fighting for Ephraim, and it cost forty-two thousand lives.

And here is where I have to stop preaching at Ephraim and look at the church, because the Shibboleth test never died, it just changed words. We still build little fords of the Jordan and station ourselves at the crossing and demand that people pronounce our words our way before we will count them as ours. The right vocabulary. The right secondary doctrine. The right political instinct, the right cultural shibboleth, the right accent of faith, and if a brother says it slightly wrong, we do not slaughter him at the river, but we do something with our contempt that is close enough to grieve the Spirit. Notice that the Ephraimites and the Gileadites spoke the same language. This was not a Hebrew failing to understand a foreigner. It was one Hebrew detecting another Hebrew by the smallest possible difference and using that difference to kill. That is exactly how tribal contempt works inside the household of faith, it does not need a real heresy; it only needs a mispronounced vowel, a slightly different emphasis, a brother who frames the same gospel in a dialect that is not ours. "A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city" (Proverbs 18:19). I have stood at that ford. I have made men prove they were my kind before I would receive them, and called it discernment when it was tribalism. The church has spent more energy killing its own over Shibboleths than it has ever spent reaching the Ammonites outside.

This is the horror the whole book has been building toward, God's people indistinguishable from the violence they were called to be different from. And it is the reason the cry underneath Judges grows louder with every chapter: someone has to make these brothers one again, because they will not do it themselves. The answer, when He comes, will be a King who prays not that His people would win their arguments but "that they may all be one" (John 17:21), and who makes the warring tribes into one body not by a purity test at the river but by His own blood, which "has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14). The wall Ephraim and Gilead built with corpses, He tears down with a cross. There is no Shibboleth at His ford. There is only His blood, which speaks a better word than the blood crying up from the Jordan.

Israel's worst enemy is Israel.

## A Promise Made to People Who Stopped Asking
*Grace that arrives before anyone thinks to cry out*

**Text:** Judges 13:1–25 · **Supporting:** Romans 5:8 · Ezekiel 16:6 · Ephesians 2:4–5 · Isaiah 65:1

By the time we reach Samson, the cycle of Judges has worn down to its lowest groove, and the most telling detail in chapter thirteen is what is missing. Every previous oppression ended with Israel crying out to God. Not this one. "The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, so the Lord gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years" (Judges 13:1), and then, silence. No cry. No groaning. No turning. Israel has sunk so deep it does not even ask anymore. And it is precisely there, into that silence, that God speaks the promise of a deliverer. This is grace at its most unsettling, grace that comes to people who stopped reaching for it.

**Grace into the silence**
Forty years of Philistine domination, and Israel makes no appeal. Compare that to every other oppression in the book, under Cushan they cried out, under Eglon they cried out, under Midian they cried out, and the absence here is deafening. The well of even that desperate prayer has gone dry. The people are not pleading; they are not even complaining. They have made their peace with the Philistines the way the comfortable always make their peace with their captivity.

And the angel of the Lord appears anyway, not to a king, not to a priest, not to the nation, but to a nameless barren woman in an obscure town. "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son" (Judges 13:3). Barrenness on top of silence, a closed womb among a closed-hearted people, and God chooses exactly that emptiness to plant a deliverer. He did not wait for Israel to ask. Isaiah would later put God's own words to this kind of mercy: "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me" (Isaiah 65:1). The initiative is entirely God's. The deliverance begins before anyone wants it.

**Set apart from the womb, and already shadowed**
The angel sets the boy apart before he is conceived: "the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines" (Judges 13:5). No wine, no unclean food, no razor on his head, consecrated from the first cell. Manoah, the father, begs for the angel to return and teach them how to raise this child, and the angel does, and then ascends in the flame of their sacrifice (13:20). It is a chapter full of glory. The barren conceive. Heaven speaks. A deliverer is named and set apart and blessed, and "the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him" (13:25).

And yet, read it with the rest of the book in your hands and you feel the shadow already lying across the cradle. He shall *begin* to save Israel, only begin, not finish, and we will learn why. The Nazirite vow is announced with such care precisely because every term of it will be broken: he will touch the dead, he will feast and drink, he will let a woman cut his hair. The signs of hope come already darkened by what this man will not keep. The grace is unconditional in its arrival and tragic in its handling, and the chapter wants you to hold both, that God moved freely toward people who had stopped asking, and that the vessel He chose was flawed from the first chapter to the last.

**The God who moves first**
This is the gospel hiding in a birth announcement, and it indicts our whole instinct about how God works. We assume the order is: we want Him, we seek Him, we ask, and then He comes. Chapter thirteen reverses it. He came to a people who had stopped asking, through a womb that could not produce, with a grace nobody requested. That is not the exception in Scripture. That is the pattern. "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Not when we cried out. Not when we cleaned up. While we were still in it, not even asking. Ezekiel paints the picture without sparing us, Israel as a newborn abandoned in a field, kicking in its own blood, and God passing by and saying, "Live!" (Ezekiel 16:6). We did not call to Him from that field. We could not. He spoke first.

And I need this more than I want to admit, because I am most often the silent Israelite, not the crying one. The honest truth about spiritual deadness is that it does not feel like crisis. It feels like settling in. You stop asking not in a moment of dramatic rebellion but in a slow accommodation, until the silence feels normal and you would not even know to call it captivity. If God only came to people who were reaching for Him, He would never have come to me, because by the time He moved I had stopped reaching. "But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:4–5). Even when we were dead. The dead do not ask. He came anyway.

So before there is a single thing in this chapter about what Samson should have done, there is everything about what God simply did. He moved toward a barren woman in a forgotten town for a people too numb to pray, and He did it because that is who He is, the God who is ready to be found by those who were not even looking. Whatever silence you are in, He is not waiting on your cry to begin.

God moves before we ask.

## The Strong Man Ruled by His Appetites
*Spirit-given power governed by the eyes and the temper*

**Text:** Judges 14:1–15:20 · **Supporting:** Galatians 5:16–17 · 1 John 2:16 · Proverbs 25:28 · 2 Peter 2:19

Samson is the strongest man in the Bible and one of the weakest. That is the whole paradox of his story, and chapters fourteen and fifteen lay it open. The Spirit of the Lord rushes upon him and he tears a lion apart with his hands; he strikes down thirty men, then a thousand more with the jawbone of a donkey. Real power, divinely given. And the same man is led around by his eyes and his anger like a bull with a ring in its nose. He has the gift and not the government of it, and the book is teaching us, slowly and painfully, that a man can be filled with God's Spirit in his strength and ruled by his flesh in his soul.

**"She is right in my eyes"**
It starts the way it will end, with what he sees. Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine woman, and comes home with one demand: "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife" (Judges 14:2). His parents object, she is one of the uncircumcised; the law warned against exactly this. And Samson's answer is the thesis of his entire life: "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes" (14:3). Right in my eyes. The very phrase the book will use as its final indictment over all Israel, every man doing what was right in his own eyes, is here the personal creed of its last judge. Samson is Israel in one body: gifted, set apart, and governed by appetite.

He breaks his Nazirite vow almost immediately. He kills the lion, and later scrapes honey from its carcass and eats it, a Nazirite touching the dead, defiling himself for a snack, and he does not even tell his parents what he has done (14:8–9). Then comes the wedding feast, *mishteh*, a drinking feast, where a man under a vow against wine has no business being. The pattern is set: every consecration God placed on him, Samson treats as negotiable the moment his appetite speaks.

**Strength in service of his temper**
Then the riddle, the betrayal, the rage. Samson poses a riddle to the Philistines, they pressure his wife, she pries it out of him, and when he loses the bet his response is not justice but fury: "the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men... and gave their spoil to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). Watch that carefully, the Spirit empowers, and Samson spends the power on a tantrum. His wife is given to another man, and Samson catches three hundred foxes, ties torches to their tails, and burns up the Philistines' fields. They retaliate by burning his wife and her father. He answers with more slaughter, "he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow" (15:8). It is a feud, escalating, personal, drenched in injured pride. And underneath every act of strength is a man who cannot govern himself for a single chapter.

And God still uses it. This is the strange grace the narrator keeps noting, "it was from the Lord, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines" (Judges 14:4). God bends even Samson's lust and rage toward the deliverance of Israel. But do not mistake God's sovereignty for God's approval. That He can steer a selfish man toward a good end does not sanctify the selfishness. Samson strikes the Philistines, yes, and he never once strikes the thing that is actually destroying him, which is himself.

**A city with broken-down walls**
Here is the diagnosis Scripture gives, and it fits Samson like a glove: "A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls" (Proverbs 25:28). All his strength is in his arms; there are no walls around his soul. The Philistines could not breach him, but his own eyes and temper walked in through the open gap whenever they pleased. Paul names the war directly: "the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other" (Galatians 5:17). And John lists the three siege engines that took Samson down, "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16). He saw, he wanted, he raged, he avenged. Every gate fell from the inside.

Now the mirror, because this is the most modern chapter in the book and the one I most need to preach to myself. We have made a god of the gifted man. We will excuse almost anything in someone with obvious power, the talent, the charisma, the strength that gets results, and we call the gift the proof of God's favor, when the gift was never the point. Samson had the Spirit's power on his arms and no holiness in his heart, and the church keeps producing his sons: gifted leaders, anointed and undisciplined, strong in the pulpit and ruled by their appetites in the dark. I have watched it end careers and homes, and I know the soil it grows in, because the same split runs through me, the temptation to trade the slow work of self-government for the quick proof of a visible gift. "Whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved" (2 Peter 2:19). The strongest man in the world was a slave, and his chains were his own desires.

And this is why Samson, of all the judges, points so sharply to the Deliverer he could never be. Samson had power and no self-mastery. Christ had infinite power and total self-mastery, He who could have called twelve legions of angels held still under the lash, who was led not by His eyes but by His Father's will, who walked toward death by appetite for nothing but obedience. "I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me" (John 6:38). Samson destroyed others in his strength and himself along with them. Christ laid His strength down and saved the very people who broke Him. The gift was never enough. We needed the One who could govern it.

Gifted and undisciplined still destroys.

## Blind, Bound, and Finally Praying
*Grace that meets a man in the ruins of his own making*

**Text:** Judges 16:1–31 · **Supporting:** Luke 15:17 · 2 Corinthians 12:9 · Psalm 51:17 · Hebrews 11:32–34

Samson's story ends in a Philistine temple, blind, chained, his hair shorn, a spectacle for his enemies' entertainment, and it is there, in the total ruins of a wasted life, that he prays for the first time the Scripture records. That is the terrible mercy of chapter sixteen. The man who treated holiness as a game loses everything the game was supposed to protect, and in the losing, finally, he turns to God. This is not a triumph. It is a rescue from the wreckage, and it tells us something about how grace most often finds us.

**The slow theft of everything**
The chapter is a study in degrees of loss. First Delilah, hired by the Philistine lords to learn the secret of his strength, works him like a field. Three times he lies to her, and three times she springs the trap on him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" (Judges 16:9), and three times he should have known, and three times he stays. He is playing. He thinks he can flirt with the edge of his vow forever and always walk away strong. "She pressed him hard with her words day after day, and his soul was vexed to death. And he told her all his heart" (16:16–17). He treated the holy thing as a toy until the toy became his executioner.

And then the most chilling sentence in the book. The last lock of hair is cut, the Philistines seize him, and "he did not know that the Lord had left him" (Judges 16:20). He did not know. He rose to shake himself free as before, expecting the power to be there, and it was gone, and he could not feel the difference until it was too late. That is what sin does to the soul over time, it does not announce the moment God's strength withdraws. You go on assuming the presence, performing the old confidence, and the well has been dry for a while and you are the last to know. They gouge out his eyes. They bind him with bronze shackles. They set the strongest man in the world to grinding grain in a mill like an animal. Blind, bound, and shaved, every gift God gave him, gone.

**The first real prayer**
But the narrator slips in one quiet line that changes everything: "the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved" (Judges 16:22). Not as magic, the Philistines could see his hair growing and were not worried, because the hair was never the source. It was the sign of the vow. The growing hair signals a heart turning back. And at the great feast to Dagon, with three thousand on the roof mocking the blind man led out to amuse them, Samson prays. For the first time in his entire story, he asks God for something instead of taking it: "O Lord God, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God" (Judges 16:28). Remember me. Strengthen me. Please. The arrogant man who said *she is right in my eyes* now has no eyes, and from the dark he finally asks. He braces against the pillars, and "the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those he had killed during his life" (16:30).

Read the prayer carefully. It is not yet a perfect prayer, there is still a cry for vengeance for his two eyes in it. But it is a true one, because it is the prayer of a man with nothing left to trust but God. That is the only kind of prayer the proud ever learn, and they usually learn it in the ruins. "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). God did not despise the broken man chained to a millstone. He answered him.

**Grace in the ruins**
Here is the gospel pressed into the rubble of a collapsed temple. Grace did not meet Samson at the height of his strength. It met him at the bottom of his folly, blind, humiliated, stripped of every gift, with nothing to offer but a prayer. The prodigal in the far country had to reach the pigsty before "he came to himself" (Luke 15:17), and so did Samson, and so, if we are honest, do most of us. We do not run to God from the mountaintop. We crawl to Him from the wreckage of the life we built without Him. "My power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Samson never knew that until he had no power of his own left to trust.

And I will not stand over this man, because his pattern is too close to my own and to everyone I have buried under their secret sins. We are all betting, like Samson, that we can play at the edge of holiness and always walk away strong, that we will feel it the moment God's hand lifts, that the consequences are for other people. And the most frightening thing is not the fall. It is the not knowing, going on in the old confidence after the Spirit has quietly withdrawn, the last to feel the difference. If there is mercy in this chapter for me, it is that God is not finished even with the man chained to the mill. The hair grows back. The prayer comes. The door is still open, even from the dark.

But notice what it cost. Samson had to die to win his greatest victory, and even that came through ruin. And so the book leaves us aching for a stronger Deliverer who would also win His greatest victory through death, not through the wreckage of His own folly, but through the perfection of His obedience. Where Samson pulled the temple down on himself and his enemies in a cry for vengeance, Christ let the temple of His own body be pulled down by His enemies, praying not strengthen me against them but "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Samson killed more in his death than in his life, and so did Christ, but the death of Christ does not crush His enemies under the rubble. It saves them. The true Strong Man dies, and the people who broke Him walk out alive.

Grace meets us in the ruins.

## A Religion Built to Order
*Homemade gods for a people who do what is right in their own eyes*

**Text:** Judges 17:1–18:31 · **Supporting:** Exodus 20:4 · Isaiah 44:14–17 · Romans 1:25 · John 4:24

The judges are finished. The last five chapters of the book turn from deliverers to a portrait of what Israel has actually become down at the level of ordinary religious life, and it is grotesque. Chapters seventeen and eighteen tell the story of a man named Micah who manufactures his own gods, hires his own priest, and builds a private religion to his own specifications, only to have an entire tribe steal the whole operation. There is no foreign oppressor here. There is no dramatic sin. There is just a deeply religious Israelite doing what seems right to him, and the result is idolatry all the way down. The narrator gives us the key in a refrain that now begins to toll: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 17:6).

**The do-it-yourself shrine**
Micah's religion is a tangle of contradictions, and that is the point. He confesses to stealing silver from his own mother, returns it, and she, in the same breath, dedicates it "to the Lord" and uses it to commission "a carved image and a metal image" (Judges 17:3–4), in direct violation of the second commandment: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image" (Exodus 20:4). The name of the Lord is invoked over an act of flat disobedience to the Lord. Micah builds a shrine, makes an ephod and household idols, and "ordained one of his sons, who became his priest" (17:5), homemade clergy, no call, no tribe, no authority but his own. He is using the right words. He is sincere. He may genuinely believe he is worshiping Yahweh. And every single piece of it is invented to suit himself.

Then a wandering Levite comes through, and Micah upgrades, a real Levite is better than a son, so he hires him: ten pieces of silver a year, clothes, and food (Judges 17:10). And listen to Micah's theology, because it is the theology of every manufactured religion: "Now I know that the Lord will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest" (17:13). The Lord will prosper me. The whole apparatus exists to secure his own blessing. God has been reduced to a system Micah operates for his own benefit. He is not worshiping God. He is managing Him.

**Worship as theft and convenience**
Then the Danites arrive, a tribe still looking for territory, and they see Micah's setup and simply take it. They steal the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the priest along with them, and the Levite, offered a bigger congregation, switches employers without a flicker of conscience: "Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?" (Judges 18:19). His gladness is the giveaway. The priest goes where the prospects are better. When Micah protests that they have taken his gods, the Danites threaten him, and he goes home, and the verdict on his entire enterprise is devastating in its plainness: "What more have I? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'" (18:24). His gods could be carried off by a raiding party. He made them; someone stronger took them. The tribe of Dan sets up the stolen idol and worships it "all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh" (18:31), there was a real house of God the whole time, and Israel preferred the convenient counterfeit down the road.

Isaiah would later mock this exact absurdity to the bone: a man cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and warm himself, "and the rest of it he makes into a god... and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, 'Deliver me, for you are my god!'" (Isaiah 44:16–17). Half the log is firewood and half is your god, and you cannot see the joke because you built the thing. That is Micah. That is Dan. That is the religion you make to order, gods you carve, who cannot save, who can be stolen by anyone stronger than you.

**The god you can carry**
Now turn the mirror, because the homemade religion is not ancient at all. We do exactly what Micah did, in more sophisticated materials. We assemble a god to our own specifications, keep the verses we like, file off the commands that cost us, hire the teaching that tells us we will be prospered, and we use the name of the Lord over the whole construction, and we are sincere about it. "They exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). The most dangerous idolatry has never been the obvious kind. It is the kind that calls itself Christianity, uses the right words, attends the right building, and is built end to end around securing my blessing, my comfort, my prospering. I have to watch it in myself most of all, because a pastor can build the most elaborate Micah-shrine of anyone, a whole religion of God-talk arranged to flatter the man running it. A god you can manage is a god you have made, and a god you have made cannot save you. It can only be carried off by the next thing stronger than you.

The whole sorry chapter is screaming for a King, and the refrain tells you why. With no king, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, and what was right in their own eyes was a god the size of their own appetites. The cure is not a better shrine. It is the true King, who does not let us carve Him to order, who says, "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24), and who comes not as an idol we manage but as the Lord who manages us. Micah's god was stolen by a raiding party. The true King was killed by His enemies and walked out of the grave, because no power is stronger than Him. You cannot carry Him off. You can only bow.

Homemade gods cannot save.

## The Night Israel Became Sodom
*A covenant people now indistinguishable from the evil they were sent to drive out*

**Text:** Judges 19:1–30 · **Supporting:** Genesis 19:4–8 · Hosea 9:9 · Romans 3:10–18 · Genesis 6:5

This is the chapter most pastors skip, and that is precisely why it must be preached. Judges 19 is one of the darkest passages in all of Scripture, the gang rape and dismemberment of a defenseless woman by the people of God, and the narrator does not flinch, because he needs you to see something you would rather not. He has been building toward this since chapter one, tracking Israel's slow descent from incomplete obedience down through idolatry and civil war, and now he forces the verdict into the open: Israel has become Sodom. The nation called to be holy is now indistinguishable from the wickedness it was sent to drive out. "In those days, when there was no king in Israel" (Judges 19:1), the refrain returns, and this time it introduces an atrocity.

**The deliberate echo of Sodom**
A Levite and his concubine, traveling home, choose to lodge in Gibeah, a town of Benjamin, an Israelite town, chosen precisely because it was Israelite. "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel" (Judges 19:12). The irony is the whole point. They avoid the Gentile city to be safe among their own people, and their own people are the danger. An old man takes them in, and then: "the men of the city, worthless fellows, surrounded the house, beating on the door. And they said to the old man... 'Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him'" (19:22).

If that sentence sounds familiar, it is meant to. It is almost word for word the men of Sodom pounding on Lot's door: "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them" (Genesis 19:5). The narrator is laying the two scenes side by side on purpose. Gibeah is Sodom now. The city God rained fire on for its wickedness has a twin, and the twin is in the tribe of Benjamin, inside the covenant, inside the promised land. The very evil the conquest was meant to purge out of Canaan has set up house in Israel and is beating on the door.

**The horror the narrator refuses to soften**
What follows is unbearable, and the text means it to be. The host offers his own daughter and the concubine to the mob, itself a horror, a man bargaining with a woman's body, and in the end the Levite seizes his concubine and puts her out to them, and "they knew her and abused her all night until the morning" (Judges 19:25). At dawn she crawls back to the threshold and falls with her hands on the doorstep, and the man who should have protected her tells her coldly, "Get up, let us be going. But there was no answer" (19:28). She is dead. He loads her body on his donkey, takes her home, and dismembers her into twelve pieces, sending them throughout Israel. And the narrator gives the nation's own stunned reaction as the closing line: "such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt... consider it, take counsel, and speak" (19:30).

The Scripture does not look away, and neither may we. There is no hero in this chapter. The mob is monstrous; the host is craven; the Levite is a coward who saved himself by sacrificing the woman in his care and then butchered her body for political effect. Every man in the story fails the woman, and she has no name, and no one speaks for her until the narrator forces the whole nation to look at what it has become. This is what Israel is now, with no king and every man his own law, not merely disobedient, but cruel, and cruel to the most vulnerable person in the room.

**The line we want to draw, and cannot**
We want to read this and stand outside it, comfortably appalled, certain we are nothing like Gibeah. That instinct is the very thing the chapter exists to break. Hosea looked back at exactly this episode and used it to indict his own generation: "They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah" (Hosea 9:9), as in the days of Gibeah, meaning the rot did not stay in chapter nineteen; it is the pattern of the human heart whenever God is not King. And Paul, building his case that no one is righteous, reaches for the same darkness: "their feet are swift to shed blood; in their paths are ruin and misery" (Romans 3:15–16), and concludes, "None is righteous, no, not one" (3:10). Genesis gave the diagnosis at the start of it all: "every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). That is not Gibeah's heart. That is the heart, and Gibeah is only what the heart does when nothing restrains it.

So I will not preach this from a safe distance, because the lesson of Gibeah is that there is no safe distance. The difference between the men of Gibeah and the men in this room is not a difference of nature. It is the difference of restraint, of grace, of law, of the Spirit, of the King we have and they did not. Strip those away, give the heart no king but itself and no law but its own eyes, and Gibeah is not a foreign country. It is the basement of every one of us. The most chilling thing the chapter says about Israel is that it had become Sodom without ever noticing the moment it crossed over. That is how it happens. Not in a leap. In a long descent that always feels, from inside, like normal life.

And this is why the book is now screaming for a King with everything it has. The horror of Judges 19 is the horror of a world where no one is safe because no one is ruled, where the strong devour the weak and call it Tuesday, where the people of God are no better than Sodom because nothing rules their hearts. The cry for a king is not a cry for politics. It is a cry for a righteousness that comes from outside us, because we have just watched what we are without it. The King we needed came at last, and the first thing the true King did was draw near to the abused and the nameless and the thrown-away, the very people Gibeah destroyed. He did not put the vulnerable out to the mob to save Himself. He put Himself out to the mob to save the vulnerable. The Levite handed over the woman to die in his place; the Lord handed over Himself to die in ours.

Without God, no one is safe.

## Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes
*The whole book's verdict, and the King we are still waiting for*
