**Text:** Judges 20:1–21:25 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 14:12 · Isaiah 53:6 · Jeremiah 17:9 · Revelation 19:16

The book of Judges does not end with a deliverance. It ends with a nation tearing itself apart and then scrambling, by lies and abduction, to undo the worst of the damage, and then it stops, on a single sentence that is the verdict over everything that came before. There is no judge in these final chapters. There is no rescue. There is only the spectacle of a covenant people doing what is right in their own eyes all the way to the edge of self-destruction, and a narrator who refuses to let you leave without naming what you have watched.

**A holy war against a brother**
The outrage at Gibeah finally moves Israel to act, but watch how. The nation that was silent through forty years of idolatry assembles four hundred thousand men "as one man" (Judges 20:1) to punish Benjamin. There is a kind of righteousness here; the crime demanded justice. But Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men and instead defends them, and the result is civil war, Israelite against Israelite, brother against brother, the same horror as the Shibboleth slaughter now multiplied into the tens of thousands. Israel inquires of the Lord and is told to go up, and is defeated, twice, before the victory comes. And when it comes, it is total: Benjamin is all but annihilated, "and they did not spare the people" (20:35), reduced from a tribe to six hundred surviving men hiding at a rock. The people of God have nearly erased one of their own tribes from existence. The instinct to do right, untethered from God's wisdom, became its own atrocity.

**The lawless scramble to fix it**
And then the most pathetic sequence in the book. Israel, having sworn an oath not to give their daughters to Benjamin, suddenly grieves that a tribe will vanish, and sets about solving the problem with more bloodshed and abduction. They slaughter the entire town of Jabesh-gilead for failing to join the war, sparing four hundred virgins to hand to the Benjaminites as wives (21:10–12). When that is not enough, they coach the remaining men of Benjamin to hide in the vineyards at Shiloh and seize the dancing girls of the festival as they come out, kidnapping as a wedding arrangement, sanctioned by the elders (21:20–21). They are not consulting God anymore. They are managing a disaster with their own cleverness, and every solution is a fresh sin. The fixing is as lawless as the breaking. This is what it looks like when men do what is right in their own eyes even in their repentance, even their attempts at justice are crooked, because the crookedness is in them.

**The verdict over everything**
And then the book ends. No resolution, no deliverer, no rest for the land. Just the refrain one final time, now stripped of all comfort and standing as the judgment over the whole eight-hundred-year descent: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). That is the last line. That is the verdict. The problem was never only the Canaanites, or Midian, or the Philistines. The problem was Israel's own heart with no king to rule it. Every man his own law, every man his own eyes, every man his own god, and the result is the wreckage we have walked through for twenty-one chapters.

The phrase is a trap, and it is meant to spring on us. "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (Proverbs 14:12). Right in his own eyes, that is the most natural and the most fatal posture of the human heart, and it never feels like rebellion from the inside. It feels like sincerity. It feels like following your conscience. And Jeremiah tells you why that is not enough: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). The eyes that feel so sure are the eyes of a sick heart. Self-rule is not freedom. It is the slow road to Gibeah, and to civil war, and to a kidnapping at Shiloh dressed up as a solution.

Now the turn the whole book has been driving toward, and it is for us, not just for them. We are the people who believe the answer is more authenticity to ourselves, that if we could just be true to what is right in our own eyes, we would be free. Judges spent twenty-one chapters showing you where that road ends. I have walked it. I have done what was right in my own eyes and called it conviction, and I have managed the wreckage afterward with more sin, and patched my failures with cleverness instead of repentance, and every one of those repairs needed repairing. "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way" (Isaiah 53:6). Every one to his own way. That is the book of Judges in eight words, and it is the diagnosis of the whole human race.

But read the rest of that verse, because it is the answer the book itself could not give: "and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). The endless cry of Judges, no king, no king, no king, is finally a cry the gospel answers. Israel did not need a better judge; the cycle ate the best of them. Israel did not need a king like the nations; the next book will show that kings fail too. Israel needed the King who is also the Lamb, who does not merely rule the rebellious heart from above but takes its iniquity into Himself and gives it a new heart from within. The book ends with no king on purpose. It ends with a wound it cannot heal, so that you will go looking for the One who can, the King whose robe is written "King of kings and Lord of lords" (Revelation 19:16), who rules not by abduction and slaughter but by a cross, and who does for us the one thing no judge in Israel ever could. He does not just deliver us from our enemies. He delivers us from ourselves.

We need a King who saves.
